cards.q: How should you choose which data role to aim for?
cards.a: Read five real job descriptions for each role and list the tools. The tools show the real work. Do not choose from titles or social media hype, and do not wait until you know everything.

cards.q: Why build your skill gap list from 10 real job descriptions instead of a 'top 20 skills' blog post?
cards.a: Real JDs for your target role and city show demand. Count and rank the skills: if only 2 of 10 JDs mention Kafka, it is a later skill. A famous list pushes you to study Spark, Kafka and Kubernetes all at once.

cards.q: At what gaps do you review flashcards, and how many new cards a day is sensible?
cards.a: Review at 1, 3, 7, 14 and 30 days. Add only 3 to 5 new cards a day, from things you got wrong. Thirty new cards a day for a week creates 210 reviews you cannot finish.

cards.q: What is the rule for video time versus practice time, and the test that you have really learned something?
cards.a: For every 20 minutes of video, spend 40 minutes doing. If you could not do it with the video closed, you have not learned it. 'I watched the course' is not practice.

cards.q: What do PREP and STAR stand for, and when do you use each?
cards.a: PREP is Point, Reason, Example, Point, for explanations: say the answer first. STAR is Situation, Task, Action, Result, for behavioural stories. At about 130 words a minute, a 60-second answer is about 130 words.

cards.q: You are asked for a deadline you cannot confirm. What builds more trust than saying yes?
cards.a: A polite 'Let me check and reply by 2 pm.' A wrong yes that misses the deadline costs more trust. Likewise, say 'my guess is...' when you are guessing, so a senior person is not surprised later.

cards.q: Where should the ask and the conclusion go in a work email?
cards.a: Put the ask in the subject and the conclusion in the first line, with evidence in bullets and a dated next step. A hidden ask in paragraph four makes the reader reply 'what do you need?' and costs a day.

cards.q: What makes a good question in a work chat?
cards.a: State the goal, what you tried, expected versus actual, and a minimal example. Paste the full error as text in a code block, not a screenshot, so people can search and copy it.

cards.q: Churn fell from 4% to 3%. How do you word it, and why is 'fell 1%' risky?
cards.a: Say 'fell 1 point, from 4% to 3%' or 'fell 25%'. 'Fell 1%' can be read as 4% to 3.96%. When a percentage can be read two ways, add both end values in brackets.

cards.q: Why can you not average +50% and -50%, and what is the overall change?
cards.a: Changes multiply. 100 becomes 150, then 75, a 25% loss overall, and 1.5 x 0.5 = 0.75. Likewise never average regional rates: go back to counts and divide totals.

cards.q: What should you do in the first minutes of a coding interview question?
cards.a: Do not code in the first 30 seconds. Spend 3 to 5 minutes clarifying, restating, giving examples, and stating the brute force first. Then optimise, code, test and state the complexity.

cards.q: A build worked at build 1 and fails at build 1,000. How many tests does bisecting need?
cards.a: log2(1,000) rounded up is 10 tests, because 2 to the power 10 is 1,024. Test build 500: if it fails, the bug is in 1 to 500. Change one thing at a time.

cards.q: Why use 'I' in STAR stories, and how should you handle a failure story?
cards.a: 'We found the bug' hides your contribution, so say what you did. Never blame a person in a failure story: name the process gap. Action is the longest part, about 200 to 260 words for 2 minutes.

cards.q: When should you start mock interviews, and why?
cards.a: From about week 6 of the 12-week plan, even if you do badly. You will never feel ready. Track one fix at a time, and try each problem for 25 minutes before reading any solution.

cards.q: State Little's law with units. A service handles 500 requests per second at 200 ms each. How many are in flight?
cards.a: L = arrival rate x time in system. 500 per second x 0.2 s = 100 requests in flight. Write units beside every number: mixing milliseconds and seconds is the classic slip.

cards.q: What is wrong with a fixed-window rate limiter, and what is a better design?
cards.a: A client can send the full limit at 11:59:59 and again at 12:00:00, doubling the rate across the boundary. Use a token bucket or a sliding window, with atomic updates in Redis.

cards.q: In an ML system design interview, what do you ask before drawing the model box?
cards.a: The metric and the data freshness. Define the online business metric first: optimising clicks offline may not improve purchases. Then follow the framework: data, features, model, serving, monitoring, with a number for every box.

cards.q: Why is accuracy or ROC alone a poor way to judge a fraud model?
cards.a: Fraud is rare, so a model that flags nothing is highly accurate. Compute precision and alert volume at the real base rate, and choose the threshold by cost at that threshold.

cards.q: What are the three passes for reading a paper?
cards.a: Pass 1: filter in about 10 minutes. Pass 2: understand in about an hour. Pass 3: rebuild only the few that matter. The abstract is advertising, so check the experiments table before you believe it.

cards.q: You run 20 independent tests at the 5% level. What is the chance of at least one false positive?
cards.a: 1 - 0.95^20 = about 64%. Each test is a new chance of luck. Correct for many tests or confirm the winner on fresh data.

cards.q: What makes a resume bullet strong, and what must you never do with its number?
cards.a: Verb, what, how, a measured result with a number, and the scale. Percent change = (old - new) / old x 100, so 40 to 10 minutes is 75%. Never invent or inflate a number: interviewers ask how you measured it.

cards.q: What should a project README show on its first screen?
cards.a: The result and a demo, plus a command that reproduces it. Then architecture, data, method, decisions and limits, and next steps. 'This project does X' with no way to run it and no numbers does not help.

cards.q: A recruiter says 'we will send the offer letter next week'. Should you resign now?
cards.a: No. Resign only after the signed offer letter, with any background-check conditions in writing. Read your notice terms before applying, and write a handover. Stay in your current role until then.

cards.q: What makes a cold referral message work?
cards.a: One named role, one proof link with a number, and an easy way to decline. 'Hi, please refer me, any opening works' costs the reader effort. Score yourself 1 point each for name, role, proof, link and easy exit.

cards.q: Only 3% of loans default. Why is 'nobody defaults' a bad model, and which metric should you use?
cards.a: It is 97% accurate and worthless, because it finds no defaulter. Use recall, precision and expected loss in rupees, where expected loss = PD x LGD x EAD.

cards.q: A pass rate moves from 92% to 95%. Is that +3% or +3 points? How should you state a domain metric?
cards.a: It is +3 percentage points (about +3.3% relative). Always say which. State a metric with its definition: 'monthly logo churn is 2%: customers cancelled in the month divided by customers at its start'.

cards.q: How do you decide whether a certification is worth taking?
cards.a: Count, in 10 job posts for your target role, how many require it. If 0 or 1, skip it; if 6 or more, plan one. Certificates are receipts, projects are the meal: five certificates with no project cannot answer 'what have you built?'.

cards.q: What should you do in the first 30, 60 and 90 days in a new data role?
cards.a: Learn in the first 30 days, deliver one small win by 60, then own a piece by 90. Do not propose a big redesign in week two: learn why things are built this way, then propose changes with your own numbers.

cards.q: Fix the sentence and name the rule: 'I am working here since 2021.'
cards.a: 'I have been working here since 2021.' Since or for with something still true now takes the present perfect continuous (or present perfect), not the present continuous.

cards.q: Fix the sentence: 'Yesterday I have sent the mail.' Why is it wrong?
cards.a: 'Yesterday I sent the mail.' A stated finished time such as yesterday or in 2021 needs the past simple. The present perfect has no stated time and the result matters now.

quiz.q: You want to move into a data role. Which is the best way to decide which skills to learn first?
opts: Follow a popular 'top 20 skills' list and study every item together
Wait until you know everything on the skill map before you apply
Count the tools in ten real job descriptions for your target role
Learn whichever tools are trending on social media this month
quiz.why: A gap list should come from demand for your target role and city: count, rank, and start with the most frequent skills. A famous top-20 list ignores your target, and skill maps are maps, not to-do lists that must be finished before applying.

quiz.q: You made 50 flashcards from one video, and reviews are piling up. What is the best fix?
opts: Cap new cards at 3 to 5 a day and delete the ones you do not need
Review all 50 cards every day until you know every one of them perfectly
Double your daily review time so that the pile clears much more quickly
Stop using flashcards altogether and re-watch the video once every week
quiz.why: Cards pile up, reviews become a burden and learners quit. Recall works when the load is small and focused on real gaps. Re-watching the video is re-reading, which the chapter ranks below recall.

quiz.q: Your manager asks whether you can deliver by Friday and you are not sure. Which reply builds the most trust?
opts: Yes, no problem, I will manage it somehow
I will try my best, but I cannot promise anything at all
That is not possible, the plan was unrealistic from the start
Let me check the dependencies and reply by 2 pm today
quiz.why: A short, dated promise to answer is honest and specific. Saying yes to avoid conflict and then missing the deadline damages trust more. A vague 'I will try' gives the manager nothing to plan with.

quiz.q: Which email subject line follows good written-communication practice?
opts: Question about something I was thinking about during the weekly review
Approval needed by Fri 5 pm: extra cloud budget for the load test
Regarding the project, and a few more updates from our side of the work
Hi, hope you are doing well, I have a quick request for you when free
quiz.why: The ask, the deadline and the topic are in the subject, so the reader knows what to do before opening it. The other subjects hide the ask. Being direct is not rude: it saves the reader's time.

quiz.q: Conversion rose from 4% to 5%. Which sentence is correct and unambiguous?
opts: It rose 1%, from 4% to 5%, so conversion barely moved
It rose 20%, because the gain was 1 out of 5
It rose 1 point, from 4% to 5%, a 25% relative increase
It rose 25 points, because 1 point is a quarter of the old 4% value
quiz.why: The gap is 1 percentage point, and relative to the starting 4% it is 1/4 = 25%. Dividing by the new value (1/5 = 20%) is the tempting slip. Writing '1%' is ambiguous, so give both end values.

quiz.q: Region A had 10 conversions from 20 visits. Region B had 98 from 980. What is the overall conversion rate?
opts: 10.8%, from 108 conversions over 1,000 visits
30%, the simple mean of the two regional conversion rates
50%, because the better region sets the overall rate
5.4%, the overall rate divided between the two regions
quiz.why: Averaging averages ignores the denominators. Region A is 50% and B is 10%, so the mean of rates is 30%, but A has only 20 of the 1,000 visits. Go back to counts: 108 / 1,000 = 10.8%.

quiz.q: Checkout revenue fell 20% last week. What is the best first step?
opts: Assume the main competitor's big sale caused it and plan a matching discount
Split revenue into orders times average order value, then check data quality
Rewrite the pricing model right away, because price is the main revenue lever
Wait one more week and see whether revenue simply recovers by itself again
quiz.why: Jumping to a cause is the classic mistake. Splitting the metric and checking data quality first shows where the drop is and whether it is real. List hypotheses with a test for each before acting.

quiz.q: In a behavioural interview you say 'We found the bug and we fixed it.' What is the problem?
opts: Using 'we' is better in interviews, because it shows humility and good teamwork
It is too short, so you should add the full project backstory before the result
You should name the colleague who introduced the bug, to be fully transparent
It hides your own contribution, so describe what you did with 'I'
quiz.why: Interviewers are hiring you, so they need to hear your actions. Credit the team, but say 'I traced the duplicates to the retry; my teammate reviewed the fix.' Never blame a person: name the process gap.

quiz.q: A service handles 500 requests per second and each takes 200 ms. On average, how many requests are in the system?
quiz.why: Little's law: L = 500 x 0.2 s = 100. Dividing rate by time gives 2,500, and forgetting to convert 200 ms to seconds gives 100,000. Use the result to size workers, for example 100 / 0.7 target utilisation.

quiz.q: A fixed-window limiter allows 100 requests per minute. A client sends 100 requests at 11:59:59 and 100 more at 12:00:00. What happens?
opts: The second burst is blocked, because the one-minute window has not yet ended
Only 100 pass, because the limiter really counts a rolling minute window
Both bursts are blocked, because 200 exceeds the limit
All 200 pass within a second, so use a token bucket or sliding window
quiz.why: A fixed window resets at the boundary, so each burst lands in a different window and both are allowed. That doubles the intended rate for a moment. A token bucket or sliding window counts across the boundary.

quiz.q: You are asked to design a recommender system. What should you ask first?
opts: Which model architecture to use, such as a deep neural ranking network
How many GPUs the team can buy for the training of the model
Which business metric to improve and how fresh the data must be
Which vector database to use for storing all of the embeddings
quiz.why: Metric and data come before the model. Drawing the model box first, or naming tools, is the common mistake. The answers set the funnel of retrieval and ranking, the latency budget and the evaluation plan.

quiz.q: Your method beats the baseline by 0.3 points in one run, while run-to-run noise is about 0.5 points. What can you claim?
opts: Nothing yet: run several seeds and report the mean and spread
Your method is better, because it scored higher than the baseline here
The baseline is weak, so you should leave its settings at default
Keep trying different seeds until the gap looks clearly larger
quiz.why: A gain smaller than the noise is not evidence: in the chapter's simulation single runs fooled the reader about 19% of the time. Tuning the seed is cherry-picking, and leaving the baseline untuned is an unfair comparison.

opts: Responsible for improving the performance of data pipelines in the team
Cut nightly runtime from 40 to 10 minutes (75%) by batching warehouse writes
Worked on Spark, Kafka, dbt, Snowflake and Kubernetes pipelines for several teams
Improved pipeline performance by 90% through major optimisation work across stages
quiz.why: It has a verb, a measured result, a number and a method, and it can be defended in a 2-minute story. A duty statement and a tool list have no result. A round, unmeasured 90% invites the question 'how did you measure that?'.

quiz.q: A recruiter says on a call, 'We will send your offer letter next week.' What should you do about your notice?
opts: Resign now, so that your notice period starts running a few days earlier
Tell your manager about the verbal offer to see how they react to it
Wait for the signed offer letter and its written conditions before resigning
Resign, and ask the recruiter to confirm the offer by email later
quiz.why: A verbal promise is not an offer: terms can change or the offer can be withdrawn. Resign only on a signed letter with any conditions in writing. Starting the notice early only helps if the offer is certain.

quiz.q: A loan has PD 2%, LGD 50% and EAD of Rs 10,00,000. What is the expected loss?
quiz.why: Expected loss = PD x LGD x EAD = 0.02 x 0.5 x 10,00,000 = Rs 10,000. Rs 20,000 forgets LGD (only PD x EAD), and Rs 5,00,000 forgets the probability (LGD x EAD). Always state the three inputs.

quiz.q: How should you decide whether to invest in a certification?
opts: Check 10 job posts: plan one if 6 or more require it, skip it if 0 or 1
Buy the single most popular certificate to be safe, whatever the jobs ask
Collect several cheap certificates quickly to fill up the resume page
Skip every certificate, because projects are the only thing that count
quiz.why: Let demand decide: the job posts for your target role show whether a certificate is required or just preferred. Collecting badges without a project does not answer 'what have you built?'. Rejecting all of them ignores real filters.

quiz.q: You still work at the company you joined in 2021. Which sentence is correct?
opts: I have been working here since 2021.
I am working in this company since 2021.
I work in this company since the year 2021.
I was working in this company since 2021.
quiz.why: Since 2021 starts in the past and is still true now, so you need the present perfect continuous (or present perfect). The present continuous and present simple do not link the past to now, and the past continuous suggests it has ended.

quiz.q: Which sentence about a future possibility is correct?
opts: If I will get time, I will help.
If I would get time, I will help.
If I get time, I will help.
If I am getting time, I will help.
quiz.why: After 'if', use the present simple even when the meaning is future, and keep 'will' for the result. Putting will, would or a continuous form in the if-part is a common learner error.
